vignette: Ahmad, a 55-year-old Middle Eastern man and farmer, had been struggling to cope with the aftermath of an assault that occurred six months ago. Married for over three decades, Ahmad’s life has revolved around his farm and family. The traumatic event happened while he was alone in one of his fields. A group of masked individuals approached him, threatening him and ultimately assaulting him severely. Since then, any sign of a heart racing or the smell of sweat brings back fragmented memories that make him feel like he is reliving the assault. One day while working in the field, Ahmad’s heart began to race as he sensed someone following him. The olfactory trigger of sweat and the perceived threat of people acting suspiciously immediately sent him spiraling into a state of intense anxiety. These triggers have led him to ruminate extensively about how to get even with his assailants, often imagining scenarios where he could confront them again but this time defend himself. Ahmad’s memories of that day are fragmented pieces that do not fit together, and when he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread and cannot finish. This disjointed recollection makes it hard for him to process what truly occurred during the assault. He often feels like these memories belong to someone else rather than himself, which further exacerbates his sense of disconnection from reality. Ahmad’s inability to fully connect with his experiences has driven him toward maladaptive strategies such as rumination and overworking. The more fragmented and alien his memories become, the more he throws himself into work to keep his mind occupied. He avoids anniversaries related to the event but finds that even mundane tasks like farming can trigger intense feelings of anxiety. The cycle becomes increasingly apparent when Ahmad returns home exhausted after a long day in the fields, only to find himself ruminating about how to exact revenge on those who attacked him. This relentless focus on the assault and his assailants consumes much of his mental energy, making it difficult for him to engage meaningfully with his wife or enjoy simple pleasures that once brought him joy. Ahmad’s work performance has also been affected; he often becomes so engrossed in his tasks that he neglects important farm maintenance. His rumination about revenge and avoidance behaviors have strained relationships within the community, as he frequently avoids social gatherings and events tied to the anniversary of the assault. What finally brought Ahmad to seek help was a growing realization that his constant preoccupation with getting even had taken over his life. He is most afraid of losing control and ending up in a similar situation again, but at the same time, he hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy and peace. His fragmented memories and intense triggers have made it nearly impossible for him to function without feeling like every moment could be another assault waiting to happen. Ahmad is seeking help because he wants to break free from this cycle and find a path back to living his life fully, rather than constantly reliving the trauma in his mind.
